intricate

/IN-trih-kit/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Intricate means made of many small, carefully interconnected parts or details.

The watchmaker bent over the intricate mechanism, where more than a hundred tiny gears and springs had to mesh perfectly for the watch to keep time.

Example

The palace's tiled ceiling was so intricate that visitors often lay flat on the floor to trace its thousands of interlocking geometric patterns.

Thousands of small patterns interlocking into one grand design show exactly what intricate means: detailed and complicated, with many parts connected to one another.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

complex: Complex means made of many connected parts, and it stays neutral: a complex system may be elegant or a mess. It measures how much there is to understand. Intricate goes further, picturing fine parts carefully interlocked, and it carries admiration for delicate, skilled construction.

elaborate: Elaborate means worked out with great detail and planning, like an elaborate scheme or an elaborate costume; it stresses the effort and ambition poured in. Intricate stresses the fineness of the result: many small parts meshing precisely into one careful design.

convoluted: Convoluted means twisted and hard to follow, and it is a criticism: a convoluted explanation loses its listener in needless tangles. Intricate is usually praise for detail mastered and organized. When the parts stop serving a design and start defeating the reader, intricate has become convoluted.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

simple: plain and easy to understand

straightforward: uncomplicated and direct

Where it sits · how interwoven its many parts are — detailed → intricate → labyrinthine

detailed vs. intricate: A detailed drawing includes many small features, while an intricate one weaves those details into a complicated, interconnected design.

labyrinthine vs. intricate: An intricate plot keeps you paying close attention, but a labyrinthine one is so tangled that even careful readers get lost.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, into

Root — tric-

Root — tric-: from Latin tricae, tangles or perplexities

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: forms adjectives

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin intricare, 'to entangle': in- (into) plus tric- (tangles) plus the adjective ending -ate describes something you could get tangled up in, full of interwoven parts.

Use the root in a new word: extricate

Use the root in a new word: extricate: It took the climber nearly an hour to extricate her rope from the high branches.

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday and academic

Intricate is usually admiring or neutral: 'intricate carvings,' 'an intricate plot,' 'intricate negotiations.' Unlike convoluted, which criticizes something for being needlessly tangled, intricate often praises careful, detailed craftsmanship.
